# Introduction

The ELEFAN functions of TropFishR (`ELEFAN`, `ELEFAN_SA` and `ELEFAN_GA`)
estimate the parameters of the von Bertalanffy growth function (VBGF) from
length-frequency (lfq) data [@taylor_extending_2017]. They return a single best
set of parameters, but no information about how certain these estimates are.
Uncertainty arises from the sampling of the lfq data (which fish were measured)
and from the optimisation itself (different runs can end in different local
optima).

Bootstrapped ELEFAN [@Schwamborn2019] quantifies this uncertainty: the lfq data
is resampled many times, ELEFAN is fitted to each resampled data set, and the
distribution of the resulting estimates is used to derive the most likely
parameters and their confidence intervals. The growth parameters of each
resample can then be used in the following steps of a length-based stock
assessment, so that the uncertainty is propagated to mortality rates and
reference points. This vignette shows how to

1. resample lfq data (`lfqResample`),
2. run bootstrapped ELEFAN (`ELEFAN_GA_boot`, `ELEFAN_SA_boot`),
3. summarise and plot the results (`univariate_density`, `LinfK_scatterhist`,
   `vbgfCI_time`, `plotBoot`),
4. estimate natural, total and fishing mortality, selectivity and reference
   points for each resample (`M_empirical`, `MstochThen`, `catchCurve`, `VPA`
   and `predict_mod` with the argument `boot`).

The [ELEFAN tutorial](https://cran.r-project.org/package=TropFishR/vignettes/Using_TropFishR_ELEFAN_functions.html)
explains the ELEFAN functions and their settings in more detail.


# Data

We use the synthetic data set `synLFQ7`, which was simulated with known growth
parameters (see `?synLFQ7`): $L_\infty$ = 123 cm, $K$ = 0.2 year$^{-1}$,
$C$ = 0.3, $t_s$ = 0, and recruitment around April ($t_{anchor}$ between 0.16
and 0.34). Knowing the true values allows us to judge the bootstrapped
estimates.

```{r data, fig.height = 7, fig.cap = "Length-frequency data of synLFQ7: (a) catches and (b) restructured data with a moving average over 9 length classes (MA = 9)."}
library(TropFishR)
data(synLFQ7)
lfq <- synLFQ7

## true parameters of the simulation
true_par <- c(Linf = 123, K = 0.2, C = 0.3, ts = 0,
              phiL = log10(0.2) + 2 * log10(123))

MA <- 9
op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(lfq, Fname = "catch")
plot(lfqRestructure(lfq, MA = MA), Fname = "rcounts")
par(op)
```

The moving average (`MA`) can significantly affect the results
[@taylor_extending_2017]. As a rule of thumb, it should approximate the number
of length classes spanned by the smallest (youngest) cohort and has to be an
odd number (see the ELEFAN tutorial). Here, `MA = 9` separates the cohorts well.


# Resampling of length-frequency data

`lfqResample` draws, for each sample (date), as many fish as were measured,
with replacement and with probabilities proportional to the observed
frequencies. A resampled data set therefore has the same number of fish per
sample, but different frequencies by length class:

```{r resample, fig.height = 7, fig.cap = "Restructured length-frequency data: (a) original and (b) resampled data."}
set.seed(1)
lfq_resampled <- lfqResample(lfq)

## same number of fish per sample
totals <- rbind(original = colSums(lfq$catch), resampled = colSums(lfq_resampled$catch))
colnames(totals) <- format(lfq$dates, "%d %b")
totals

op <- par(mfrow = c(2, 1), mar = c(4, 4, 1, 1))
plot(lfqRestructure(lfq, MA = MA), Fname = "rcounts")
plot(lfqRestructure(lfq_resampled, MA = MA), Fname = "rcounts")
par(op)
```

The differences between the original and the resampled data reflect how
different the data could have been if other fish of the same population had
been measured.


# Bootstrapped ELEFAN

`ELEFAN_GA_boot` resamples the data `nresamp` times and fits `ELEFAN_GA` to
each resampled data set; `ELEFAN_SA_boot` does the same with `ELEFAN_SA`. Most
arguments are passed on to `ELEFAN_GA` or `ELEFAN_SA`. As for single ELEFAN
fits, the search space (`low_par`, `up_par`) and the moving average (`MA`)
have to be adjusted to the data:

```{r settings}
## lower and upper limits of the search space
low_par <- list(Linf = 100, K = 0.01, t_anchor = 0, C = 0, ts = 0)
up_par <- list(Linf = 160, K = 3, t_anchor = 1, C = 1, ts = 1)
## genetic algorithm: population size, maximum number of generations, number of
## generations without improvement before stopping, probability of mutation
popSize <- 60
maxiter <- 50
run <- 10
pmutation <- 0.2
## number of resamples
nresamp <- 200
```

Each resample takes as long as a single ELEFAN fit, so the bootstrap takes a
while: with the settings above, about 20 minutes on a single core. The
resamples are independent and can be fitted in parallel (`parallel = TRUE`)
on `no_cores` cores. For the parallel version, TropFishR has to be installed,
because each core loads it. The argument `outfile` allows following the
progress in a text file. The `seed` makes the results reproducible:

```{r bootstrap, eval = FALSE}
res <- ELEFAN_GA_boot(lfq, MA = MA, seasonalised = TRUE,
                      low_par = low_par, up_par = up_par,
                      popSize = popSize, maxiter = maxiter, run = run,
                      pmutation = pmutation,
                      nresamp = nresamp, seed = 1,
                      parallel = TRUE, no_cores = 7)
```

```{r load_bootstrap, include = FALSE}
## The bootstrap above is not run when building the vignette (it takes too
## long); the results were precomputed with the same code.
res <- readRDS("synLFQ7_boot.rds")
```

To keep this vignette short to build, the results were precomputed with the
code above. We used 200 resamples here; for real assessments, more resamples
(e.g. 500 or more) give more stable confidence intervals.


# Results

The result is an object of class `lfqBoot`. Its element `bootRaw` contains the
estimates of each resample:

```{r bootRaw}
head(res$bootRaw)
```

The growth performance index $\phi' = \log_{10}(K) + 2 \log_{10}(L_\infty)$
(`phiL`) and the maximum age (`agemax`) are derived from $L_\infty$ and $K$.
Each resample is identified by its seed (`res$seed`) and has a score
(`res$Rn_max`).

The estimates are summarised by a multivariate kernel density estimate:
`maxDen` is the parameter combination with the highest density, i.e. the
most likely combination, `median` the median of each parameter, `CI` the
univariate (here 95 %) confidence intervals and `multiCI` the range of each
parameter within the multivariate 95 % confidence region:

```{r summary}
res$maxDen
res$CI
```

Compared to the true parameters:

```{r comparison}
pars <- c("Linf", "K", "C", "ts", "phiL")
round(data.frame(true = true_par[pars],
                 max_density = res$maxDen[pars],
                 median = res$median[pars],
                 CI_lower = res$CI["lo", pars],
                 CI_upper = res$CI["up", pars]), 3)
```

The confidence intervals of $L_\infty$ and $K$ include the true values, and the
growth performance index $\phi'$ is estimated very precisely. The seasonal
parameters $C$ and $t_s$, on the other hand, are very uncertain: their
confidence intervals span almost the whole search space. Note that $t_s$ is
periodic ($t_s$ = 0 is equivalent to $t_s$ = 1). Such wide intervals are
exactly the information that a single ELEFAN fit does not provide.


# Graphs

## Distributions of the parameters

`univariate_density` shows the distribution (kernel density) of each
parameter with the confidence interval (dashed lines) and the value with the
maximum density (solid line). Known true values can be added with the argument
`truePar` (red dashed lines). The values in this plot are based on the
univariate density of each parameter; they can therefore differ slightly from
`res$maxDen` (multivariate density) and `res$CI` (quantiles):

```{r univariate, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 5.5, fig.cap = "Distributions of the bootstrapped estimates with 95 % confidence intervals (dashed black lines), maximum density (solid lines) and the true values (dashed red lines)."}
univariate_density(res, truePar = true_par, mfrow = c(2, 4))
```

## Correlation of Linf and K

Estimates of $L_\infty$ and $K$ are typically negatively correlated, i.e.
similar growth curves can be described by a large $L_\infty$ with a small $K$
and vice versa. `LinfK_scatterhist` shows the joint distribution of both
parameters. Isolines of the growth performance index $\phi'$ can be added
with `phi.contour = TRUE` (or to any $L_\infty$-$K$ plot with `add_phiprime`).
A few resamples ended with much larger values of $K$ (up to
`r round(max(res$bootRaw$K), 1)`); the plot is limited to $K \le 1$ with
`ylim`:

```{r scatterhist, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 6, fig.cap = "Bootstrapped estimates of Linf and K (points), their bivariate kernel density (shading and contours) and isolines of the growth performance index (dashed grey lines)."}
LinfK_scatterhist(res, phi.contour = TRUE, ylim = c(0, 1))
```

## Growth curves

`vbgfCI_time` shows the growth curves of all resamples (grey lines) over
relative time together with the confidence intervals of the curves and the
growth curve with maximum density:

```{r vbgfCI, fig.cap = "Growth curves of the bootstrapped estimates (grey), the 95 % confidence interval (dashed lines) and the growth curve with maximum density (solid line)."}
ci <- vbgfCI_time(res, agemax = 15, perm.col = adjustcolor("grey50", 0.2))
```

`plotBoot` shows the same growth curves with confidence intervals in the
length-frequency data, one cohort per year (here limited to an age of 6
years with `agemax`):

```{r plotBoot, fig.width = 7, fig.cap = "Length-frequency data with the growth curves with maximum density (solid lines) and their 95 % confidence intervals (dashed lines)."}
plotBoot(lfq, res, agemax = 6)
```

The estimates with maximum density can also be used like the results of a
single ELEFAN fit, e.g. with `lfqFitCurves`:

```{r fitcurves, fig.width = 7, fig.cap = "Restructured length-frequency data with the growth curves with maximum density."}
lfq_rest <- lfqRestructure(lfq, MA = MA)
plot(lfq_rest, Fname = "rcounts")
tmp <- lfqFitCurves(lfq_rest, par = as.list(res$maxDen[c("Linf", "K", "t_anchor", "C", "ts")]),
                    draw = TRUE, col = 4, lty = 1, lwd = 2)
```


# Reproducing resamples

Resample `x` uses the seed `seed + x` (stored in `res$seed`). `lfqResample`
with the argument `boot` re-creates the resampled data sets, e.g. to inspect
the data of a resample with an unusual estimate:

```{r reproduce}
lfq_resamples <- lfqResample(lfq, boot = res)
length(lfq_resamples)

## resample with the smallest Linf
i <- which.min(res$bootRaw$Linf)
res$bootRaw[i, ]
```

The fit of a single resample can be reproduced by setting its seed, resampling
the data and fitting `ELEFAN_GA` with the same settings (the random numbers of
the genetic algorithm follow those of the resampling):

```{r reproduce_fit, eval = FALSE}
set.seed(res$seed[i])
lfq_i <- lfqResample(lfq)
fit_i <- ELEFAN_GA(lfq_i, MA = MA, seasonalised = TRUE,
                   low_par = low_par, up_par = up_par,
                   popSize = popSize, maxiter = maxiter, run = run,
                   pmutation = pmutation, plot.score = FALSE)
unlist(fit_i$par)
```


# Bootstrapped stock assessment

The functions `M_empirical`, `catchCurve`, `VPA` and `predict_mod` accept the
bootstrapping results with the argument `boot`. They apply the method to each
resample, using the growth parameters of the resample and, for `catchCurve`,
`VPA` and `predict_mod`, the resampled data set itself (re-created with the
seeds stored in the `lfqBoot` object). Each step adds its estimates as
columns to `bootRaw` and their maximum density (the mode of the univariate
kernel density), median and confidence interval to `maxDen`, `median` and
`CI`. Resamples that cannot be analysed in a step (e.g. because no
descending limb of the catch curve is found or the natural mortality exceeds
the total mortality) get `NA`, and a warning gives their number. The uncertainty of the growth
parameters is thus propagated through the whole assessment. For
`catchCurve`, `VPA` and `predict_mod`, `lfq` has to be the data set that was
used for the bootstrapped growth analysis.

In addition to the growth parameters, the simulation of `synLFQ7` used a
natural mortality of $M$ = 0.2 year$^{-1}$, a fishing mortality of
$F$ = 0.3 year$^{-1}$ (i.e. $Z$ = 0.5 year$^{-1}$), a length at 50 %
probability of capture of $L_{50}$ = 35 cm and a length at maturity of
$L_{mat}$ = 30.8 cm (see `?synLFQ7`).

## Natural mortality

`M_empirical` with `boot` estimates the natural mortality rate for each
resample with the empirical formulas based on growth parameters
("Then_growth" or "Pauly_Linf"). The new column is called `M_Then` (or
`M_Pauly`):

```{r M}
res <- M_empirical(method = "Then_growth", boot = res)
round(rbind(maxDen = res$maxDen[c("K", "M_Then")], res$CI[, c("K", "M_Then")]), 3)
```

Empirical estimators are uncertain themselves. `MstochThen` additionally
accounts for the uncertainty of the formula of @Then2015: for each resample,
M is estimated with coefficients of the formula that were refitted to a
bootstrap sample of the original data of @Then2015 (see `?MstochThen`). This
results in wider
confidence intervals. With `resid = TRUE`, the scatter of the individual
species around the formula is included as well, which describes the
uncertainty of M for a single stock better but results in much wider
confidence intervals. Each resample uses its own seed (`res$seed`, or see the
argument `seed`), so the results are reproducible:

```{r MstochThen}
res_stoch <- MstochThen(res)
res_resid <- MstochThen(res, resid = TRUE)
round(rbind(formula = res$CI[, "M_Then"], stochastic = res_stoch$CI[, "M_Then"],
            residuals = res_resid$CI[, "M_Then"]), 3)
```

## Total and fishing mortality and selectivity

`catchCurve` with `boot` applies the length-converted catch curve to each
resampled data set, with the catches summed over the samples of a year (see
the arguments `yearSel` and `yearCombine` for data covering several years).
The points used for the regression line are chosen automatically for each
resample (see `?catchCurve`). With `calc_ogive = TRUE`, the selectivity
($L_{50}$, $L_{75}$) is estimated as well, and with `natMort` the fishing
mortality is calculated as $F = Z - M$:

```{r catchCurve}
res <- catchCurve(lfq, boot = res, calc_ogive = TRUE, natMort = "M_Then")
pars <- c("Z", "FM", "L50", "L75")
round(rbind(maxDen = res$maxDen[pars], res$CI[, pars]), 3)
```

`plotBoot` with `pType = "cc"` shows the catch curves of all resamples
together with the regression line with maximum density and its confidence
band:

```{r plotcc, fig.cap = "Catch curves of the resamples (grey points and lines), regression line with maximum density (black line) and 95 % confidence band (blue)."}
plotBoot(boot = res, pType = "cc")
```

The estimates of total mortality ($Z$ = `r round(res$maxDen[["Z"]], 2)`) and
selectivity ($L_{50}$ = `r round(res$maxDen[["L50"]], 1)` cm) are close to the
true values. The fishing mortality with maximum density
($F$ = `r round(res$maxDen[["FM"]], 2)`), however, is lower than the true value
(0.3), because the empirical formula overestimates the natural mortality of
this population ($M$ = `r round(res$maxDen[["M_Then"]], 2)` instead of 0.2).
The true value is within the confidence interval, but the bootstrap only
describes the uncertainty arising from the data and the assessment steps; it
does not correct for a biased natural mortality estimate.

## Yield per recruit and reference points

`predict_mod` with `boot` applies the Thompson and Bell model to each
resample, with the growth parameters, natural and fishing mortality and the
selectivity of the resample. The length class including $L_\infty$ of the
resample is the plus group. It requires the parameters of the length-weight
relationship (`a` and `b`; here with the weight in g, `LW_unit = "g"`) and, for reference points based on the spawning
potential ratio (SPR), the length at maturity (`Lmat`, with `wmat` the width
of the maturity ogive):

```{r ypr}
lfq$a <- 0.015
lfq$b <- 3
lfq$Lmat <- 30.8
lfq$wmat <- 5

res <- predict_mod(lfq, type = "ThompBell", FM_change = seq(0, 3, 0.05),
                   boot = res, natMort = "M_Then", LW_unit = "g")
pars <- c("F01", "Fmax", "F05", "F04", "SPR")
round(rbind(maxDen = res$maxDen[pars], res$CI[, pars]), 3)
```

The reference points are the fishing mortalities at which the slope of the
yield per recruit curve is 10 % of its slope at the origin (F01), the yield
per recruit is maximal (Fmax), the biomass per recruit is 50 % of the
unfished biomass per recruit (F05), and the SPR is 40 % (F04). `SPR` is the
spawning potential ratio at the current fishing mortality. The columns
`FF01`, `FFmax`, `FF05` and `FF04` give the current fishing mortality
relative to the reference points; values below 1 indicate that the current
fishing mortality is lower than the reference point. Because they are
estimated for each resample, the probability that the current fishing
mortality exceeds a reference point can be derived directly:

```{r status}
pars <- c("FF01", "FFmax", "FF05", "FF04")
round(rbind(maxDen = res$maxDen[pars], res$CI[, pars]), 3)
## probability that the current F exceeds the reference points
round(colMeans(res$bootRaw[, c("FF01", "FFmax", "FF05", "FF04")] > 1, na.rm = TRUE), 2)
```

```{r plotypr, fig.cap = "Yield per recruit curves of the resamples (grey lines), the curve of the resample with the Fmax closest to its maximum density (black line), the distribution of Fmax (histogram) and its 95 % confidence interval (blue)."}
plotBoot(boot = res, pType = "ypr", pRef = "Fmax")
```

Instead of the selectivity estimated by the catch curve, the fishing
mortality at length estimated by a length-based virtual population analysis
can be used. The VPA requires the total catch of the stock, while `lfq` has
to keep the sampled numbers of fish, because the resampling draws the
measured fish. The total landings (in kg, one value per sample) are therefore
passed to `VPA` with the argument `landings`, and each resample is raised to
the total catch (see `?VPA` and `?lfqRaise`):

```{r vpa, eval = FALSE}
landings <- rep(30000, length(lfq$dates))  # landings in kg per sampling date
res <- VPA(lfq, boot = res, natMort = "M_Then", landings = landings, LW_unit = "g")
res <- predict_mod(lfq, type = "ThompBell", FM_change = seq(0, 3, 0.05),
                   boot = res, natMort = "M_Then", bootSel = "VPA", LW_unit = "g")
```

With `bootSel = "VPA"`, `FM_change` and the reference points refer to the
maximum fishing mortality at length, which is also used as the current
fishing mortality for `SPR` and `FF01`, ....
